body.heading: Energy on the move
paragraphs: A food chain is a simple map of who eats whom. It starts with producers — plants and algae that capture sunlight — followed by herbivores that eat them, then carnivores that eat the herbivores. The arrows in a food-chain diagram point the way energy flows: from the food to the eater.

Take a meadow: grass is eaten by a grasshopper, the grasshopper by a frog, the frog by a snake, and the snake by a hawk. Each link depends on the one before it, which is why removing one species can ripple through a whole habitat.

body.heading: Why chains stay short
paragraphs: At every step, most of the energy is lost. An animal uses much of its food just to move, grow and stay warm, so only about a tenth of the energy passes on to whatever eats it. That steady loss is why food chains rarely have more than four or five links.

It also explains the shape of nature: there is far more grass than grasshoppers, more grasshoppers than frogs, and only a few hawks. Big fierce animals are rare because the energy reaching the top is thin.

body.heading: Chains join into webs
paragraphs: Real life is messier than a chain. A frog eats flies and beetles as well as grasshoppers; owls and snakes both hunt mice. Link all the chains in a habitat together and you get a food web — a fairer picture of who depends on whom. A change anywhere in the web — a drought, a new predator, a vanished plant — is felt along every chain that touches it.
Decomposers close the loop. Fungi and bacteria break down dead plants and animals, returning nutrients to the soil so producers can start the whole flow again.

takeaway: Food chains trace energy from producers to consumers; linked together they form food webs, and only about a tenth of the energy survives each step.
